Generalised age-period-cohort models (StMoMo)

Source: R/model-wrappers.R
stmomo.Rd

Wrapper around StMoMo (Villegas, Kaishev and Millossovich 2018): age-period-cohort ("apc"), Cairns-Blake-Dowd ("cbd", logit link), Renshaw-Haberman ("rh"), M6, M7 and M8 ("m6", "m7", "m8", logit link), the Plat model ("plat", logit link) and Lee-Carter ("lc"). "rh" is StMoMo's Renshaw-Haberman model with cohortAgeFun = "1" (the default of StMoMo's rh()): log m(x,t) = a(x) + b(x) k(t) + g(t - x), a cohort effect without age modulation, not the original 2006 specification of the Renshaw-Haberman model, whose cohort effect is modulated by a second age function. Models are fitted per stratum with real ages (the lower bounds of single-year intervals; models with a cohort effect need single years of age), deaths and central exposures; for the logit-link models initial exposures are approximated as central exposures plus half the deaths, and forecast death probabilities are converted to central rates (m = -log(1 - q)). Cohorts observed in fewer than clip cells get zero weight; their fitted rates use the effect of the nearest estimated cohort. Draws come from simulate() of the fitted model (period indexes simulated as a multivariate random walk with drift, the cohort index as an ARIMA process). Predictive draws (mt_forecast(predictive = TRUE)) add Poisson variation of the deaths given the rates and the exposures, and no other observation noise.

Usage

stmomo(
  model = c("apc", "cbd", "rh", "m6", "m7", "m8", "plat", "lc"),
  clip = 3,
  gc_order = NULL,
  xc = NULL
)

Arguments

model

"apc", "cbd", "rh", "m6", "m7", "m8", "plat" or "lc".

clip

Cohorts with fewer observations get zero weight.

gc_order

ARIMA order for the cohort index. Default: c(2, 0, 0) for M7 and the Plat model, c(1, 1, 0) for the other cohort models.

xc

Age at which the cohort effect of M8 vanishes (model = "m8" only). Cairns et al. (2009) estimate it; StMoMo's m8() needs a fixed value, and its example uses the highest age of the data (89 for ages 55 to 89). Default (NULL): the highest age of the data of each fit. Forecasts can depend strongly on it; compare values in a backtest (mt_compare()) or choose one with tuned().

Value

A model specification.

Details

M6, M7 and M8 are the cohort extensions of the CBD model of Cairns et al. (2009), with x the age, xbar the mean age of the data and s2 the mean of (x - xbar)^2:

  • M6: logit q(x,t) = k1(t) + (x - xbar) k2(t) + g(t - x).

  • M7: M6 plus a quadratic age term ((x - xbar)^2 - s2) k3(t); the cohort effect has no linear or quadratic trend (constraints of StMoMo's m7()).

  • M8: logit q(x,t) = k1(t) + (x - xbar) k2(t) + (xc - x) g(t - x): the cohort effect fades with age and vanishes at age xc.

The CBD family is meant for older ages (StMoMo's examples use ages 55 to 89). For M7 the cohort index is forecast with ARIMA(2,0,0) with a non-zero mean, as in the StMoMo vignette, since its constraints remove any trend; the other cohort models use ARIMA(1,1,0) with drift, except the Plat model.

Plat model. Plat (2009) combines the CBD model with features of the Lee-Carter model. "plat" is the reduced Plat model for older ages as the StMoMo vignette defines it (Villegas, Kaishev and Millossovich 2018, Section 4): logit q(x,t) = a(x) + k1(t) + (xbar - x) k2(t) + g(t - x), built with StMoMo::StMoMo() from the vignette's age functions (1 and xbar - x, xbar the mean age of the data) and its constraint function. The constraints centre both period indexes and remove the level, the linear and the quadratic trend from the cohort effect (regression of the cohort effect on the year of birth and its square, as in Haberman and Renshaw 2011). The period indexes are forecast with a multivariate random walk with drift and the cohort index with ARIMA(2,0,0) with a non-zero mean (the vignette's Table 3). The vignette uses the logit link with initial exposures for all its models; Plat (2009) uses the log link with Poisson deaths, and for all ages adds a third period term (xbar - x)+ k3(t), which he suggests dropping when only older ages are of interest. The full model with that term is not offered. In the vignette's 50-year forecasts for England and Wales men aged 55-89, the rates of this model increase, which the vignette calls implausible: the central trend is linked to the estimated cohort effect.

References

Cairns AJG, Blake D, Dowd K, Coughlan GD, Epstein D, Ong A, Balevich I (2009). A quantitative comparison of stochastic mortality models using data from England and Wales and the United States. North American Actuarial Journal 13(1): 1-35.

Haberman S, Renshaw A (2011). A comparative study of parametric mortality projection models. Insurance: Mathematics and Economics 48(1): 35-55.

Plat R (2009). On stochastic mortality modeling. Insurance: Mathematics and Economics 45(3): 393-404. doi:10.1016/j.insmatheco.2009.08.006

Villegas AM, Kaishev VK, Millossovich P (2018). StMoMo: an R package for stochastic mortality modeling. Journal of Statistical Software 84(3): 1-38. doi:10.18637/jss.v084.i03

Examples

if (requireNamespace("StMoMo", quietly = TRUE)) {
  x <- mt_example(deaths = "single", years = 1995:2019)
  fc <- mt_forecast(mt_fit(stmomo("cbd"), x), h = 5, n_draws = 50, seed = 1)
  old <- mt_regroup(mt_set_grid(x, age = single_ages(55, 89, open = FALSE)),
                    age = single_ages(55, 89, open = FALSE))
  fc7 <- mt_forecast(mt_fit(stmomo("m7"), old), h = 5, n_draws = 50, seed = 1)
  fcp <- mt_forecast(mt_fit(stmomo("plat"), old), h = 5, n_draws = 50, seed = 1)
}
